paragraphs.heading: A layer where salt changes
paragraphs.text: A halocline is a layer in a body of water where salinity, the salt content, changes sharply with depth. The name joins the Greek words hals, salt, and klinein, to slope. It is a kind of chemical layering, found most often where fresh water from rivers or melting ice meets salty sea water. Haloclines turn up in oceans, large estuaries and fjords.

paragraphs.heading: Make one in a glass
paragraphs.text: You can make a halocline in a drinking glass. Pour fresh water slowly over salt water, using a spoon held flat at the surface so the two do not mix. A hazy layer soon appears, because light bends differently on each side of the boundary. In flooded limestone caves near the sea, lighter fresh water from land sits on top of ocean salt water, and cave divers can mistake the boundary for an air space. Swimming through it tends to stir up the layers.

paragraphs.heading: Not the same as a thermocline
paragraphs.text: People often confuse a halocline with a thermocline, a layer where the temperature changes steeply. The two can line up and together form what is called a pycnocline. Salinity directly controls how density is spread through the ocean and how the ocean is layered.

paragraphs.heading: Warm seas and cold seas
paragraphs.text: In the midlatitudes, more evaporation than rain makes surface water saltier than deep water. There, the layering comes from warm surface water, and the halocline works against stability. Such places may be prone to salt fingering, a kind of mixing that favours salt. In some high-latitude seas, such as the Arctic Ocean, the Bering Sea and the Southern Ocean, surface water is colder than deep water, and the halocline keeps the water column stable by separating top from bottom. In such cold seas, it stops warm, salty Atlantic water from mixing with the cold surface layer, which lets sea ice grow.

paragraphs.heading: Where it sits and why it moves
paragraphs.text: How deep a halocline sits depends on ocean circulation, water sources and conditions in the air above. Winds and river runoff can shift its depth and stability. In the Arctic Ocean it lies between 50 and 250 m deep, depending partly on whether the water comes from the Atlantic or the Pacific. In the Baltic, a shallow sea, it sits around 60 to 80 m down but varies a lot from year to year with wind and river flow. Changes in its position and strength can strongly affect ocean mixing, how nutrients move, and low oxygen in bottom waters.
